column1: dbms-driver|J|J3|odbc|What is the primary role of a database driver in an application?|Translate API calls into database-specific communication|Grant every caller database administrator rights|Replace all server-side authorization checks|Store every database backup permanently|A driver implements access to a database through an interface or protocol. Its presence does not establish privileges or secure query construction.|Connectivity and authority are separate concerns.

odbc-dsn|J|J3|odbc|An ODBC DSN is configured on a host. What does that normally describe?|Connection configuration for a data source|A mandatory database administrator role|A cryptographic password-hashing algorithm|A browser same-origin policy|A data source name identifies configuration used to establish a connection. Credentials and security settings need separate review.|A configured connection is not proof that a login succeeds.

connection-secret|J|J3|sqli|A connection string containing a password is committed to a public repository. What must be addressed?|Credential rotation and removal from exposed artifacts|Only reformatting the string's whitespace|Only changing the database table names|Only increasing the HTTP cache lifetime|Treat the credential as exposed, restrict its permissions, and secure storage. Deleting one current file does not remove history or existing copies.|A secret's exposure survives a cosmetic edit.

pool-reuse|J|J3|sqlperm|Why can session-level database state require care with connection pooling?|A reused connection may retain state from a prior borrower|Every borrower automatically has a new physical server|Pooling inherently parameterizes all queries|A pool forbids transactions|Reset relevant state and use supported pooling behavior. Session settings, context, or temporary state can affect later work.|Logical requests may reuse physical connections.

db-tls-validation|J|J3|tlscheat|A database client encrypts traffic but accepts any server certificate. What may remain unprotected?|Reliable server identity verification|Only the SQL keyword capitalization|Only the application's icon integrity|All symmetric encryption algorithms by definition|Encryption without proper endpoint authentication may permit interception through an impersonated endpoint.|A protected channel must lead to the intended server.

db-network-allow|J|J3|sqli|A database listener is reachable from the application subnet. What additional control still matters?|Database authentication and least privilege|Only the table names' obscurity|Only the number of application buttons|Only the browser's CORS response|Network restriction reduces exposure but does not determine what a connected principal can do.|Reachability is not authorization.

service-inventory|J|J3|wstg|A host has several database instances. Why record instance identity with a finding?|Versions and security configuration can differ by instance|All instances necessarily share every password|Instance names prove ownership of every database|Only the first instance can accept network connections|Bind evidence to the specific listener, instance, account, and database tested.|One machine need not have one uniform database configuration.

banner-version|J|J3|wstg|A network banner suggests an old database release. What supports a patch finding more strongly?|Verified build and applicable vendor advisory|The listener using its usual port|A long instance name|A screenshot of the hostname alone|Version clues can be misleading or incomplete. Verify the relevant build and applicability before claiming a known vulnerability.|Product family is not an exact vulnerable build.

access-file|J|J3|access|An application uses an Access .accdb file in a shared folder. What boundary deserves particular attention?|Filesystem access to the database file|Only the SQL Server TCP listener|Only Oracle's SYSDBA role|Only a MySQL host-qualified username|Access file deployments rely heavily on controlling the file and its copies. Do not assume a separate network database server.|Identify the actual deployment model before testing controls.

backup-exposure|J|J3|sqli|The production database requires authentication, but a public backup contains the same data. What has failed?|Protection of a secondary data copy|The syntax of every SELECT query|The uniqueness of every primary key|The size of the TCP receive window|Backups and exports need access controls, retention, and encryption appropriate to their data.|The main login is only one path to the data.

db-log-secret|J|J3|sqli|SQL tracing records full parameter values, including reset tokens. What should be reviewed?|Sensitive-value handling and log access|Only the indentation of SQL keywords|Only whether the database has a GUI|Only the column order in a harmless table|Bound parameters protect query structure but may still expose sensitive data to diagnostics.|Injection prevention is not a log privacy policy.

readonly-connection|J|J3|sqlperm|A client setting labels a connection read-only. What should an assessor verify?|Effective server-enforced permissions|Only the label's spelling|Only the driver's download count|Only the query editor's background color|Some settings express intent or affect routing rather than granting a strict security boundary. Verify the account's actual rights.|A client preference is not necessarily a server restriction.

db-schema-metadata|J|J3|sqlperm|An account sees table names in metadata but cannot SELECT their data. What is demonstrated?|Metadata visibility, not full data access|Ownership of every visible table|Operating-system root access|The ability to modify every database|Metadata and data permissions can differ. State the actual information exposed and effective capability.|Discovering a name does not establish reading its contents.

db-availability|J|J3|wstg|A permitted login attempt times out at the network layer. What conclusion is supported?|The connection did not complete under those conditions|The password is definitely incorrect|The account definitely does not exist|The database is definitely fully patched|Timeouts do not isolate authentication outcome. Record the failure and distinguish routing, filtering, service, and login behavior.|A missing response is not a credential verdict.

mssql-login-user|J|J1|sqlroles|In ordinary SQL Server instance security, how do a login and database user differ?|A login is instance-scoped; a user is database-scoped|Both always have identical privileges in every database|A login is a table; a user is a stored procedure|Users exist only in browser cookies|Server and database principals operate at different scopes. Contained users and other configurations add exceptions that must be recognized.|Do not infer database authority from an instance login alone.

mssql-dbowner|J|J1|sqlroles|A user is db_owner in one database. What should not be assumed automatically?|Membership in the server sysadmin role|Broad authority within that database|A need to review database-level risk|That database and server scopes differ|db_owner and sysadmin operate at different scopes. Other configurations can create escalation routes but require evidence.|Powerful local authority is not automatically global authority.

mssql-sysadmin|J|J1|sqlperm|Why is giving an ordinary web application SQL Server sysadmin excessive?|It grants broad instance authority beyond routine data access|It limits the app to one read-only view|It disables the ability to create any login|It forces all queries to use parameters|Choose permissions required by the workload and separate deployment administration where possible.|Convenience during setup can become persistent excessive privilege.

mssql-integrated|J|J1|sqlroles|A web app connects to SQL Server using integrated authentication. Whose effective database identity should be checked?|The identity actually presented by the connection|Always the interactive browser user's name|Always the local Administrator account|Always the database name itself|Service identity, delegation, and configuration determine the presented principal. Do not infer it from the frontend user.|Application user and database principal may differ.

mssql-role-path|J|J1|sqlperm|A user has no direct SELECT grant but can read through a role. What does this show?|Effective rights include role membership|Direct grants are the only permission source|Roles are just comments in metadata|SELECT never requires permission|Evaluate memberships and inherited permissions, not just direct grants.|A short direct-grant list is not a complete privilege inventory.

mssql-ownership|J|J1|sqlchain|A stored procedure can read a same-owner table that its caller cannot query directly. What mechanism may explain this?|Ownership chaining|HTML output encoding|DNS recursion|Password salting|Under applicable ownership-chain rules, underlying permission checks can be skipped. Review object ownership and execution context.|Effective access can flow through modules, not only direct table rights.

mssql-execute-as|J|J1|sqlchain|A SQL Server module runs with EXECUTE AS under a privileged principal. What must be assessed?|The module's reachable actions under that context|Only the caller's default text editor|Only whether the module name has a prefix|Only the browser's certificate store|Impersonated execution changes the authority available inside the module. Review permitted operations and unsafe dynamic construction.|The caller's apparent low privilege may not describe module execution.

mssql-dynamic-chain|J|J1|sqlchain|Why review dynamic SQL separately in a procedure relying on ownership chaining?|Its execution and permission behavior can differ from static statements|Dynamic SQL always receives no permissions|Static SQL cannot access tables|Every dynamic statement is automatically signed|Execution context, ownership-chain behavior, and safe parameterization require separate examination for dynamic statements.|A procedure's static path does not prove its dynamic path behaves identically.

mssql-xp-disabled|J|J1|sql|xp_cmdshell is disabled on an instance. What is supported by that fact alone?|That this feature is currently disabled|That every OS interaction is impossible|That no account has excessive privileges|That the instance has no injection flaws|Feature state is one control. Account permissions and other capabilities must be assessed separately.|A disabled command-execution feature is not a complete security assessment.

mssql-xp-context|J|J1|sql|When SQL Server xp_cmdshell runs, why inspect its execution identity?|OS consequences depend on the service or proxy context|It always runs as the browser user|It always runs as local SYSTEM|It always runs without filesystem permissions|The OS security context differs according to caller and proxy configuration. Confirm effective identity rather than assuming maximum privilege.|Database execution and OS privilege are separate facts.

mssql-linked|J|J1|linked|A linked server maps many local users to one powerful remote login. What is the concern?|Remote privileges exceed individual local requirements|The local database has too few columns|Linked servers always use anonymous FTP|Every remote query is read-only by design|Review remote identity mappings and permitted operations. Links can extend a local principal's reach into other systems.|Trace authority across connection boundaries.

mssql-contained|J|J1|sqlroles|A contained database user authenticates at database scope. What assumption should be avoided?|Every user must map to a traditional instance login|Users may have database-level permissions|Connection context affects authentication|The database can contain its own principal|Contained users are an exception to the simple login-to-user mapping model. Identify the actual authentication design.|Foundational rules often have explicit deployment-specific exceptions.

mssql-public|J|J1|sqlroles|A sensitive permission is granted to SQL Server's public database role. Who may inherit it?|All database users belonging to public|Only users whose names start with public|Only the host's local Administrator|Only accounts with expired passwords|All database users are members of public. Review its grants carefully rather than treating it as an ordinary limited group.|Broad default membership magnifies a grant.

mssql-permission-scope|J|J1|sqlperm|Which is narrower for an app needing one report: SELECT on a dedicated view or membership in db_datareader?|SELECT on the dedicated view|db_datareader for all current and future tables|Both always grant identical access|Neither can permit any read access|Granting access to a specific appropriate view can reduce exposed data compared with broad reader-role membership.|Match permission scope to the actual workload.

mssql-service-account|J|J1|sql|A SQL Server service account is also a domain administrator. Why does this increase consequence of service compromise?|The OS identity has excessive domain authority|Domain membership automatically prevents SQL injection|The database cannot use TLS|Tables become public web pages|Service identities should have only needed rights. A compromised service can act within its OS principal's authority.|Database hardening and service-account hardening reinforce each other.

mssql-auth-mode|J|J1|sqlroles|SQL Server permits both Windows and SQL authentication. What does this configuration establish?|SQL-authenticated logins can be supported|Every SQL login uses a default password|All Windows accounts become sysadmin|The server uses plaintext network transport|Authentication mode enables methods; it does not reveal actual credentials, role memberships, or channel protection.|An enabled option is not evidence of an insecure account.

mssql-revoke|J|J1|sqlperm|A direct SELECT grant is revoked, but another role still grants SELECT. What may happen?|The user retains effective read access|Revocation deletes the table|The user automatically loses every role|Every query becomes a stored procedure|Evaluate all permission paths. Removing one grant does not necessarily remove the capability.|Revocation must be checked against effective permissions.

mssql-tde-limit|J|J1|tde|Transparent Data Encryption protects database files at rest. What does it not inherently prevent?|An authorized SQL principal reading permitted data|Offline disclosure from an unprotected plaintext file|The use of encryption keys by the database engine|The need to manage encryption keys|At-rest encryption does not replace access control on live database queries. Protect keys and backups appropriately.|Encryption addresses a particular data state and threat.

mssql-backup-right|J|J1|sqlperm|An application account can back up a database containing other tenants' records. What should be investigated?|Whether backup capability exceeds its required access|Only whether table names are lowercase|Only whether the login has a profile picture|Only whether SELECT returns HTML|A backup operation may expose data outside the app's normal query surface. Review both permission and destination access.|Operational capabilities can create alternate disclosure paths.

mssql-audit-limit|J|J1|sqlperm|A query is logged successfully. Does that logging itself prevent an unauthorized read?|No; prevention depends on access enforcement|Yes; a logged query never returns data|Yes; audits automatically revoke sysadmin|No; databases cannot enforce any access controls|Audit supports detection and investigation. Permissions and other controls enforce access.|Recording an action and denying it are different functions.

oracle-schema-user|J|J2|oracleusers|In Oracle, a schema named APP exists. Must APP necessarily be an account that can log in with a password?|No; schema-only accounts can exist|Yes; every schema requires a public default password|Yes; schema names are always operating-system users|No; Oracle schemas cannot contain tables|Oracle supports schema-only accounts, including many supplied accounts in modern releases. Inspect authentication state.|An object's owner name does not prove a usable credential.

oracle-create-session|J|J2|oracle|What does Oracle CREATE SESSION principally permit?|Connecting to the database|Reading all application tables|Creating every database user|Operating-system root execution|Connection permission is separate from object and administrative privileges.|A successful login does not establish access to all data.

oracle-system-object|J|J2|oracle|How does SELECT on one table differ from SELECT ANY TABLE in Oracle?|One is object-scoped; the other is a broad system privilege|Both always apply to exactly one row|Both are browser permissions|The object grant enables all OS commands|Oracle distinguishes system and object privileges. Broad ANY privileges require careful review, including documented exclusions.|Scope and exceptions determine the real capability.

oracle-with-grant|J|J2|oracle|An Oracle object privilege is granted WITH GRANT OPTION. What additional ability does that confer?|Granting that object privilege onward|Changing the database's TLS certificate automatically|Becoming SYSDBA without further checks|Reading every OS password file|Grant option permits delegation of the granted object privilege under applicable rules.|Permission delegation expands who can receive access.

oracle-admin-option|J|J2|oracle|For Oracle role or system-privilege grants, what does WITH ADMIN OPTION affect?|Ability to grant that role or privilege to others|The pixel dimensions of the administration console|Only the order of rows returned by SELECT|Only the database backup compression ratio|ADMIN OPTION permits onward administration of the granted role or system privilege. Do not confuse it with object GRANT OPTION.|Similar grant syntax can apply to different privilege categories.

oracle-sysdba|J|J2|oracle|Why should SYSDBA access be separated from routine application access?|It provides powerful database administration authority|It is required for every ordinary SELECT|It limits the caller to their own profile|It is just a display label for a schema|Administrative authentication and privileges have substantial consequences. Routine apps should not require them.|An application's workload rarely needs full database administration.

oracle-listener|J|J2|oracleusers|An Oracle listener accepts a connection request. What does that alone prove?|Listener reachability and a handled connection attempt|Successful database user authentication|Permission to read every schema|The exact password for SYS|A listener routes connections to services; database authentication and authorization are separate stages.|A network service reply is not a database login.

oracle-service-sid|J|J2|oracleusers|Why distinguish an Oracle service name from a user name in connection evidence?|A service selects a database service, not an account|A service name is always a password|A user name identifies a TCP socket only|Every service name grants DBA membership|Connection routing identifiers and principal identifiers serve different roles. Record both where relevant.|An endpoint context does not establish a principal.

oracle-cdb-pdb|J|J2|oracleusers|In an Oracle multitenant deployment, why record which PDB is accessed?|User and privilege scope depend on container context|Every PDB necessarily shares all users and permissions|PDB names are only browser tab labels|Only the root container can hold application tables|Common and local identities, services, and grants need context. Do not generalize one container's access to all others.|Scope includes the connected container.

oracle-defaults|J|J2|oracleusers|A historical note lists SCOTT/TIGER. What should a modern assessment infer?|A legacy sample-account lead to verify, not a guaranteed login|Every Oracle installation exposes that credential|SYSDBA access is already proven|All sample schemas are enabled and unlocked|Installation, release, sample schemas, account locking, and authentication differ. Avoid asserting universal defaults.|Historical knowledge guides a check; it does not replace evidence.

oracle-locked|J|J2|oracleusers|A supplied Oracle account is locked. What is supported by this observation?|Its locked authentication state in that database|No object owned by it can ever be used|No administrator can ever change its state|The entire database has no vulnerabilities|Account state and schema-object availability are separate. Assess applicable privileges and paths.|A locked login does not erase its schema.

oracle-definer|J|J2|oracle|An Oracle stored program uses definer's rights. What authority should be reviewed?|The program's execution context and exposed operations|Only the caller's browser origin|Only the procedure name's character count|Only the default SQL worksheet font|Definer-rights code can expose capabilities beyond the caller's direct rights. Review privilege rules and safe implementation.|Calling a program can cross an authority boundary.

oracle-invoker|J|J2|oracle|What is the key distinction of an Oracle invoker-rights program?|Relevant execution authority follows the invoker context|It always executes as SYS regardless of caller|It cannot contain any SQL statements|It automatically encrypts all result rows|AUTHID and Oracle's documented resolution and privilege rules matter when assessing program behavior.|Rights mode is a security-relevant program attribute.

oracle-db-link|J|J2|oracle|An Oracle database link uses a stored remote account. What should be assessed?|Who can use it and the remote account's effective rights|Only the local table's number of indexes|Only the hyperlink color in a browser|Only the database listener's uptime|Links can extend access to a remote database under different credentials. Review visibility, authentication, and privilege scope.|Follow the identity used on the far side.

oracle-directory|J|J2|oracle|An Oracle directory object points to a filesystem location. Does an object grant alone establish that every OS file is accessible?|No; database and OS restrictions both matter|Yes; all file ownership checks disappear|Yes; every path becomes a public HTTP resource|No; directory objects cannot refer to filesystem paths|Directory-object privileges operate alongside OS permissions and feature-specific rules. Review both layers.|A database privilege does not automatically remove OS controls.

oracle-audit|J|J2|oracle|Why distinguish a failed login audit record from a successful privilege-use record?|They demonstrate different events and outcomes|All audit events prove successful compromise|A failed login always proves no such account exists|Audit text always contains the account's password|Correlate event type, result, principal, and context. Do not infer access solely from an attempt.|Attempt and success are different evidence.

mysql-account-host|J|J3|mysql|In MySQL, why can 'app'@'localhost' and 'app'@'%' differ?|User and host together identify an account|The percent sign guarantees administrator rights|Both names must share one password and all grants|Only localhost accounts can use SQL|MySQL account matching includes host context. Review the matched account rather than username alone.|A username can have multiple host-qualified identities.

mysql-grant-scope|J|J3|mysql|An app receives privileges on shop.* rather than *.*. What does this primarily narrow?|Database-object scope|The number of TCP packets per query|The character encoding of all passwords|The browser's allowed origins|Grant scope determines which databases or objects are covered. The granted privilege types still matter.|Narrow scope and narrow capabilities are both needed.

mysql-file|J|J3|mysql|A MySQL account has FILE privilege. Which consequence deserves review?|Server-side file operations within applicable restrictions|Guaranteed operating-system root authority|Automatic ownership of all tables|The ability to change every DNS record|FILE-related operations depend on server settings, filesystem permissions, and statement rules.|A powerful database feature still has environmental constraints.

mysql-local-infile|J|J3|mysql|How does LOAD DATA LOCAL differ from server-side file loading?|LOCAL can involve a file on the client host|LOCAL always reads only the server's root directory|LOCAL grants every user the FILE privilege|LOCAL is an HTML upload attribute|Review both server and client settings and the trust of the database endpoint for client-side file access.|The word local refers to the client in this feature.

mysql-prepared|J|J3|mysqlprep|Can a MySQL parameter marker replace an arbitrary table name in a prepared SQL statement?|No; markers represent data values in permitted positions|Yes; markers replace every SQL keyword|Yes; any database object is a bound string literal|No; MySQL does not support prepared statements|Use fixed mappings for permitted identifiers and bind data values through the correct API.|Query structure and query data need different treatment.

db-foreign-key|J|J3|sqli|Does a foreign key enforcing customerId existence also prove the requester may access that customer?|No; referential integrity is not user authorization|Yes; any valid customer ID is public by definition|Yes; foreign keys authenticate browser sessions|No; foreign keys never validate relationships|A relational constraint verifies a data relationship, not the application's principal-to-resource policy.|A valid reference can still be unauthorized.

db-view-filter|J|J3|sqlperm|A view hides a sensitive column, but the app can also SELECT the base table. What undermines the intended restriction?|The alternate broader grant|The view's alphabetical name|The number of rows in the view|The use of SELECT in the view definition|A restricted interface helps only if alternate permissions do not expose the protected data.|Review all available access paths.

db-encryption-app|J|J3|tde|An application decrypts sensitive columns using a key available to its own service account. What compromise still threatens plaintext?|Compromise of that authorized application context|Only loss of a ciphertext-only copy without the key|Only a misspelled table alias|Only the removal of an index|Encryption can protect stored copies while the authorized runtime remains able to access plaintext.|Evaluate where keys and decrypted data become available.

db-json-input|J|J3|sqli|An application stores JSON through a bound database parameter. Is the JSON format itself the injection defense?|No; the safe binding supplies the data boundary|Yes; JSON strings cannot contain quotes|Yes; JSON automatically removes SQL operators|No; binding only works for numeric data|Any supported value type should be safely bound. JSON text can still be unsafe when concatenated into SQL.|Data format does not replace safe query construction.

db-password-vs-data|J|J3|password|A database stores login passwords with a password hash. What should be used for a secret the app must recover verbatim?|Appropriate encryption or secret storage|The same irreversible password hash|A plain Base64 transformation|An unsalted fast checksum as encryption|Password verification does not need recovery; reusable service secrets have a different requirement and need controlled recoverability.|Choose protection according to how the value must be used.

db-migration-rights|J|J3|sqlperm|An app needs schema changes during deployment but only data operations at runtime. What design reduces runtime authority?|Separate migration and runtime principals|Keep permanent administrator access for convenience|Grant every anonymous visitor CREATE TABLE|Store the DBA password in a public JavaScript bundle|Use an appropriately controlled deployment principal and a narrower runtime identity.|Temporary deployment needs should not become permanent application privilege.

db-connection-failover|J|J3|tlscheat|A primary database connection validates certificates, but failover disables validation. What must be corrected?|Equivalent identity checks across failover paths|Only the primary server's desktop theme|Only the standby instance's name length|Only the app's public navigation labels|Security requirements apply to alternate endpoints and recovery paths too.|Availability paths can introduce weaker trust decisions.

db-export-retention|J|J3|sqli|A diagnostic export contains full customer data and persists after testing. What lifecycle control is missing?|Appropriate retention and protected disposal|Only a larger database buffer pool|Only a faster sorting algorithm|Only the choice of SQL keyword case|Temporary copies need clear ownership, protection, and retention appropriate to the task and data.|A temporary purpose does not guarantee temporary exposure.

db-parameter-log|J|J3|sqli|A query is fully parameterized. Which security property must still be enforced separately?|Authorization to the selected records|Separation of bound values from query syntax|The ability to bind supported data types|The driver's placeholder syntax|Parameterization prevents one class of query manipulation, not legitimate query access to unauthorized data.|Safe syntax is not a complete access policy.

db-privilege-retest|J|J3|sqlperm|After reducing a database account's roles, what verification is useful?|Required operations succeed and forbidden operations fail|Only that the role list is shorter|Only that the service restarts once|Only that the connection string was reformatted|Verify effective capability and application function, including inherited or alternate paths.|A permission change must achieve its intended behavior.

db-row-filter|J|J3|sqlperm|A multi-tenant app enforces tenant filtering in most queries but omits it in one export. What must be evaluated?|The export's actual tenant authorization boundary|Only whether the table has a primary key|Only whether every query uses uppercase SELECT|Only whether the server has a short hostname|Safe query construction still needs correct authorization predicates or equivalent policies on all relevant paths.|A missing business filter is not repaired by parameter binding alone.

oracle-role-disabled|J|J2|oracle|An Oracle account has a granted role that is not enabled in the current session. Why does this matter?|Granted and currently usable privileges can differ|Granted roles are always permanent SYSDBA access|Disabled roles delete every associated table|A role can never be enabled after login|Review role activation, authentication requirements, and execution context when assessing effective rights.|Inventory grants and test the relevant effective context.

db-view-write|J|J3|sqlperm|An account can SELECT a view. Does that alone prove it can UPDATE the underlying rows?|No; write rights and view behavior need separate evidence|Yes; every SELECT grant includes UPDATE|Yes; every view permits unrestricted writes|No; SQL databases never permit updates through views|Reading and writing are separate capabilities. Updatability and permissions depend on the DBMS and view.|Do not infer mutation from observation alone.

db-key-backup|J|J3|tde|An encrypted database backup is stored alongside an unrestricted copy of its decryption key. What is weakened?|Protection against theft of that combined backup set|Only the database's primary-key uniqueness|Only the SQL parser's error text|Only the ordering of report rows|Protect keys independently and control their lifecycle. Encryption offers little confidentiality when the attacker obtains the required key too.|Review the whole recovery package, not the ciphertext alone.
